assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Grossman-Helpman programme built the modern theory of trade policy as an outcome of special-interest politics, and extended trade theory into endogenous growth and innovation. It has shaped both theory and applied work on protection, trade agreements and political economy. Its reach beyond trade is broad.
assessment.attribution: The pairing is a long-standing, tightly coupled coauthorship, with the central papers and the book Interest Groups and Trade Policy written jointly. Other credited contributors to political-economy trade models are secondary. The two-name proposal is clean.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the late 1980s to the 1990s and has been confirmed over decades. Krugman's earlier prize covered adjacent trade theory but not this contribution. There is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the prize as overlapping with the earlier trade prize.
Helpman also appears in B030, so credit could be split across the two trade candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products, together with dynamic industry models, transformed empirical industrial organisation and is now routine in antitrust, merger review and regulation. It is a rare case where methods and policy practice are both changed.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand framework is mainly Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, and Pakes also has foundational dynamic-game work (Ericson-Pakes). Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin have real contributions, but the three-name limit makes this the most defensible core.
assessment.maturity: The work has been verified for three decades, with very wide adoption across fields.
uncertainties: Bresnahan's early contributions to empirical IO would be left out.
How the committee would weigh a methods prize here against applied IO.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax data reshaped how economists and the public measure and debate inequality. The work also changed research agendas in public economics and macro-distribution. Its influence on measurement is strong.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are central to the top-income series and their theory of taxation. Zucman's work on offshore wealth is important but later and could reasonably be included. The two-name proposal reflects the origin of the data programme.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from 2003 onward and has had two decades of replication, extension and criticism. The data-construction side is well established.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the wealth and top-share estimates and of the interpretation of r > g.
Whether the committee prefers to include Zucman.
Saez also appears in B045, which complicates credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their work developed the intertemporal approach to open-economy macroeconomics (Foundations of International Macroeconomics). It also identified the exchange-rate disconnect and related puzzles that frame open-economy research and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: The textbook and the exchange-rate puzzle papers are joint, with Obstfeld-Rogoff (1995, 2000) as the key references. Rogoff also appears in B011, and the committee would need to decide how to treat the overlap.
assessment.maturity: The work has had three decades to be absorbed, and the new open-economy macro models are a standard policy tool.
uncertainties: Some of the empirical puzzles remain unresolved.
Competition from other macro candidates, and from other Rogoff-related credit, may dilute support.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Social-preference models of reciprocity, fairness and inequity aversion explain experimental evidence that standard self-interest cannot, and they have been applied to contracts, labour and public goods. Fehr's experimental and theoretical work helped make the field central to behavioural economics.
assessment.attribution: The Fehr-Schmidt (1999) inequity-aversion model and Fehr's experimental programme are the core. Falk is a prominent collaborator whose inclusion is plausible, but the two-name proposal is closest to the originating contributions. Bolton-Ockenfels is not credited here, which is a gap in the attribution.
assessment.maturity: The work has been replicated and extended for more than twenty years, and it is widely taught and applied.
uncertainties: External validity of lab-based social preferences.
Relevant parallel contributions are outside the credited names.
Recent Nobel recognition of behavioural economics might temper urgency.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and the financial accelerator explain how credit frictions amplify and propagate shocks. They became the foundation of macro-financial modelling and of post-2008 policy analysis. The framework is clear and influential.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is the core, with Gertler's accelerator and later intermediary work building on it. Gilchrist is a significant empirical contributor but secondary. Bernanke's earlier prize covered related work on the banking side.
assessment.maturity: The work has had almost three decades of confirmation, and its relevance was reinforced by the financial crisis.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, which could reduce the case.
Gertler also appears in the New Keynesian candidate, B042.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance established that legal origins and investor protection systematically shape financial development and corporate governance, which reoriented comparative corporate finance and institutional economics. It has very high citation and policy impact.
assessment.attribution: The 1997-98 papers and the later legal-origins synthesis are clearly collective work by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. A three-name limit forces an exclusion, and Vishny's role is substantial.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than twenty-five years old and widely influential. Its main legal-origins claims have drawn sustained criticism over measurement and causality.
uncertainties: Contested empirical identification of legal origins.
Exclusion of Vishny.
Reputational controversies around some credited individuals, which are not a matter of scientific merit.
My own expertise is in corporate finance, so I note possible proximity bias and apply the same criteria as for other fields.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, interest-rate rules and microfounded monetary policy analysis underpins the policy models used by central banks. Its practical impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others each made distinct contributions, and a three-name limit forces hard choices. Woodford's synthesis, Taylor's rule and Gali's work on the framework are one plausible core.
assessment.maturity: The framework has had decades of application and is mature. Its performance in the recent inflation episode and the rise of heterogeneous-agent models bear on its current standing.
uncertainties: Severe attribution ambiguity among many contributors.
Calvo and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans are excluded under the three-name limit.
Debate over how well the models fit recent inflation dynamics.
